title.en: Yao Cedes the Empire to Hsü Yu (Zhuangzi)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 1, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 1

summary.en: The Golden-Age emperor Yao begs the hermit Hsü Yu to take the throne, comparing himself to a torch lit in sunshine. Hsü Yu refuses: the tit needs only one twig, the tapir only a bellyful of river; reputation is but the shadow of reality, and the empire has no need of him.
summary.zh: 堯讓天下於許由，自比燭火之於日月。許由辭之：鷦鷯巢林不過一枝，偃鼠飲河不過滿腹；名者實之賓，天下於我無所用。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The Emperor Yao wished to abdicate in favour of Hsü Yu, saying, "If, when the sun and moon are shining, you persist in lighting a torch, is not that a misapplication of fire? If, when the rainy season is at its height, you still continue to water the ground, is not this a waste of labour? Now, sir, do you assume the reins of government, and the empire will be at peace. I am but a dead body, conscious of my own deficiency. I beg you will ascend the throne."

"Ever since you, sire, have directed the administration," replied Hsü Yu, "the empire has enjoyed tranquillity. Supposing, therefore, that I were to take your place now, should I gain any reputation thereby? Besides, reputation is but the shadow of reality; and should I trouble myself about the shadow? The tit, building its nest in the mighty forest, occupies but a single twig. The tapir slakes its thirst from the river, but drinks enough only to fill its belly. To you, sire, belongs the reputation: the empire has no need for me. If a cook is unable to dress his funeral sacrifices, the boy who impersonates the corpse may not step over the wines and meats and do it for him."

title.en: The Divine Man of the Miao-ku-shê Mountain (Zhuangzi)

region.en: Miao-ku-shê mountain, a fabulous peak (symbolic pin: Songshan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 藐姑射山（神話之山；象徵定位：河南嵩山）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 1, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 1

summary.en: Chien Wu mocks the madman Chieh Yü's tale of a divine man on the Miao-ku-shê mountain — flesh like ice and snow, living on air and dew, riding clouds with dragons for his team. Lien Shu answers that such blindness is of the mind: the flood and the scorched drought cannot harm him, and out of his dust one might fashion two such men as Yao and Shun.
summary.zh: 肩吾譏接輿之言狂妄無稽；連叔答以心盲——藐姑射神人肌膚若冰雪，不食五穀，吸風飲露，乘雲氣御飛龍；洪水焦金不可害之，其塵垢秕糠猶可陶鑄堯舜。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). The immortal-on-a-sacred-mountain image became a founding vision of Daoist transcendence.

passages.text: "He declared," replied Chien Wu, "that on the Miao-ku-shê mountain there lives a divine man whose flesh is like ice or snow, whose demeanour is that of a virgin, who eats no fruit of the earth, but lives on air and dew, and who, riding on clouds with flying dragons for his team, roams beyond the limits of mortality. This being is absolutely inert. Yet he wards off corruption from all things, and causes the crops to thrive. Now I call that nonsense, and do not believe it."

"Well," answered Lien Shu, "you don't ask a blind man's opinion of a picture, nor do you invite a deaf man to a concert. And blindness and deafness are not physical only. There is blindness and deafness of the mind, diseases from which I fear you yourself are suffering. The good influence of that man fills all creation. Yet because a paltry generation cries for reform, you would have him condescend to the details of an empire!

"Objective existences cannot harm him. In a flood which reached to the sky, he would not be drowned. In a drought, though metals ran liquid and mountains were scorched up, he would not be hot. Out of his very dust and siftings you might fashion two such men as Yao and Shun. And you would have him occupy himself with objectives!"

title.en: The Five-Bushel Gourd and the Salve of Chapped Hands (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 五石之瓠與不龜手之藥（莊子）

region.en: Prince of Wu's court, Suzhou (Jiangsu, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 1, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 1

summary.en: Hui Tzü boasts of a gourd too large to be of use, which he smashed. Zhuangzi answers with the Sung silk-washer's secret salve for chapped hands: sold for a hundred ounces of silver, it won the Prince of Wu a naval victory and its seller a fief — the same drug, a different use. Float the gourd as a boat over river and lake.
summary.zh: 惠子謂莊子：魏王貽大瓠之種，樹成五石之實，無所用之而掊之。莊子舉宋人洴澼絖之秘藥：鬻技百金，吳王以之敗越，裂地而封。物之大小，繫於所用。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Hui Tzŭ said to Chuang Tzŭ, "The Prince of Wei gave me a seed of a large-sized kind of gourd. I planted it, and it bore a fruit as big as a five-bushel measure. Now had I used this for holding liquids, it would have been too heavy to lift; and had I cut it in half for ladles, the ladles would have been ill adapted for such purpose. It was uselessly large, so I broke it up."

"Sir," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "it was rather you who did not know how to use large things. There was a man of Sung who had a recipe for salve for chapped hands, his family having been silk-washers for generations. Well, a stranger who had heard of it, came and offered him 100 oz. of silver for this recipe; whereupon he called together his clansmen and said, 'We have never made much money by silk-washing. Now, we can make 100 oz. in a single day. Let the stranger have the recipe.'

"So the stranger got it, and went and informed the Prince of Wu who was just then at war with the Yüeh State. Accordingly, the Prince used it in a naval battle fought at the beginning of winter with the Yüeh State, the result being that the latter was totally defeated. The stranger was rewarded with territory and a title. Thus, while the efficacy of the salve to cure chapped hands was in both cases the same, its application was different. Here, it secured a title; there, a capacity for washing silk."

"Now as to your five-bushel gourd, why did you not make a boat of it, and float about over river and lake? You could not then have complained of its not holding anything! But I fear you are rather woolly inside."

title.en: The Gnarled Tree Too Big for the Axeman (Zhuangzi)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 1, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 1

summary.en: Hui Tzü complains that Zhuangzi's words are like his worthless tree — knotted, twisted, ignored by every carpenter. Zhuangzi contrasts the wild cat, clever and doomed to the snare, with the yak too big to catch mice and therefore safe; plant the useless tree in the domain of non-existence and repose beneath its shade, beyond the axe and all injury.
summary.zh: 惠子謂莊子言大而無用。莊子對以狸狌之死於機辟與斄牛之不能執鼠；無用之樹當樹之於無何有之鄉，彷徨乎無為其側，不夭斤斧，物無害者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Hui Tzŭ said to Chuang Tzŭ, "Sir, I have a large tree, of a worthless kind. Its trunk is so irregular and knotty that it cannot be measured out for planks; while its branches are so twisted as to admit of no geometrical subdivision whatever. It stands by the roadside, but no carpenter will look at it. And your words, sir, are like that tree;--big and useless, not wanted by anybody."

"Sir," rejoined Chuang Tzŭ, "have you never seen a wild cat, crouching down in wait for its prey? Right and left it springs from bough to bough, high and low alike,--until perchance it gets caught in a trap or dies in a snare. On the other hand, there is the yak with its great huge body. It is big enough in all conscience, but it cannot catch mice.

"Now if you have a big tree and are at a loss what to do with it, why not plant it in the domain of non-existence, whither you might betake yourself to inaction by its side, to blissful repose beneath its shade? There it would be safe from the axe and from all other injury; for being of no use to others, itself would be free from harm."
